precepts.text: Elisha tells a later king of Israel to go to the prophets of his father and his mother, showing how a true prophet of the Most High kept his distance from the corrupted worship of the northern kingdom.
precepts.point: This is the setting for a division that ran between the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom. After the split, the northern kingdom fell into idolatry and forsook the Levites, so a prophet of the Most High would want nothing to do with their manner of worship.

note.label: 1 Kings 22: A Lying Spirit and the Fall of Ahab

precepts.why:
“And Elisha said unto the king of Israel, What have I to do with thee? get thee to the prophets of thy father, and to the prophets of thy mother.”

After the kingdom split, the northern kingdom fell into idolatry, so a true prophet of the Most High kept his distance from its corrupted worship. Elisha told a later king of Israel to go to the prophets of his father and his mother; he wanted nothing to do with their manner of worship.

That is the setting in 1 Kings 22. Ahab gathered “about four hundred men” as his prophets, and they said with one mouth, “Go up; for the Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king.” These were the prophets of the northern kingdom, not the prophets of the Most High.

precepts.text: Jeroboam made two calves of gold and set them in Bethel and in Dan, telling Israel these were the gods that brought them out of Egypt, and this thing became a sin.
precepts.point: Nevertheless he cleaves to the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, and departs not from them. The house of Ahab had reared up images and led the kingdom into idolatry.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

precepts.why:
Jehoram “cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin”. Here is that sin. Jeroboam “made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” He set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, “And this thing became a sin: for the people went to worship before the one, even unto Dan.”

Jehoram the son of Ahab wrought evil, “but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made.” He put away Baal, but not the calves. The house of Ahab had reared up images and led the kingdom into idolatry, and even the son who took down Baal “departed not therefrom”: he held on to Jeroboam’s golden calves, the sin that made Israel to sin.

precepts.text: The Lord causes the enemies that rise up against Israel to be smitten before their face when the nation keeps his commandments.
precepts.point: This victory is a testament to how great a people Israel was when the hand of the Lord was with them. When Israel was in its right mind and its prayers went forth, the Lord fought for them, which is part of why the heathen nations, and Moab in particular, have hated Israel to this day.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

precepts.why:
“The Lord shall cause thine enemies that rise up against thee to be smitten before thy face: they shall come out against thee one way, and flee before thee seven ways.” That is the promise to Israel when the nation keeps his commandments, and here it is in the field against Moab.

The Moabites came out one way. Rising early, they saw the sun on the water “as red as blood” and said, “This is blood: the kings are surely slain, and they have smitten one another: now therefore, Moab, to the spoil.” They ran toward the camp expecting to gather the plunder of dead men. Instead “the Israelites rose up and smote the Moabites, so that they fled before them”, and Israel went forward smiting them even into their own country, beating down the cities, stopping the wells and felling the good trees.

This is a testament to how great a people Israel was when the hand of the Lord was with them. When Israel was in its right mind and its prayers went forth, the Lord fought for them and their enemies were smitten before their face. That is part of why the heathen nations, and Moab in particular, have hated Israel to this day.

precepts.text: Elisha says that but for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah he would not look toward the king of Israel nor see him.
precepts.point: The hatred carried straight through the history. Elisha would not even look toward the king of Israel and dealt only with Jehoshaphat of Judah, and later Pekah of Israel conspired with Rezin of Syria against Judah, which began the exile of the north by the Assyrian kings.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
The hatred carried straight through the history. Elisha told the king of Israel, “As the Lord of hosts liveth, before whom I stand, surely, were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would not look toward thee, nor see thee.”

The prophet would not even look toward the king of Israel. He dealt only with Jehoshaphat of Judah. That is the same wall Peter speaks of: a Jew did not keep company with the northern kingdom.

points: Jehoram the son of Ahab begins to reign over Israel in Samaria in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah and reigns twelve years. He works evil in the sight of the Lord, but not like his father and mother, for he puts away the image of Baal that his father had made.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Nevertheless he cleaves to the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, and departs not from them. The house of Ahab had reared up images and led the kingdom into idolatry.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Mesha king of Moab is a sheepmaster who rendered to the king of Israel a hundred thousand lambs and a hundred thousand rams with the wool, as tribute. But when Ahab is dead, the king of Moab rebels against the king of Israel.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: King Jehoram goes out of Samaria, numbers all Israel, and sends to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, telling him Moab has rebelled and asking whether he will go up with him to battle. Jehoshaphat answers, I will go up; I am as thou art, my people as thy people, and my horses as thy horses.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: They agree to go up by the way through the wilderness of Edom.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: The king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom fetch a compass of seven days' journey, and there is no water for the host or for the cattle that follow them. The king of Israel says the Lord has called these three kings together to deliver them into the hand of Moab.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Jehoshaphat asks whether there is not a prophet of the Lord that they may inquire of the Lord by him. One of the king of Israel's servants answers that Elisha the son of Shaphat is there, who poured water on the hands of Elijah.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Jehoshaphat says the word of the Lord is with him, so the three kings go down to Elisha.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Elisha confronts the king of Israel, asking what he has to do with him, and sends him to the prophets of his father and of his mother. The king answers that the Lord has called the three kings together to deliver them into the hand of Moab.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Elisha says, as the Lord of hosts liveth before whom I stand, that were it not that he regarded the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, he would not look toward the king of Israel nor see him. He addresses the matter only for the sake of the righteous king of Judah.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Elisha calls for a minstrel, and when the minstrel plays, the hand of the Lord comes upon him. He says, thus saith the Lord, make this valley full of ditches.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Though they will see neither wind nor rain, the valley shall be filled with water that they and their cattle and beasts may drink. This is but a light thing in the sight of the Lord.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: The Lord will also deliver the Moabites into their hand, and they shall smite every fenced city and every choice city, fell every good tree, stop all the wells of water, and mar every good piece of land with stones.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: In the morning, when the meat offering is offered, water comes by the way of Edom and the country is filled with water. When the Moabites hear the kings have come up to fight, they gather all who can put on armor and stand in the border.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: Rising early, the Moabites see the sun shining on the water on the other side red as blood, and conclude the kings are slain and have smitten one another. They cry, Moab to the spoil, and run toward the camp expecting to gather the plunder of dead men.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: This victory is a testament to how great a people Israel was when the hand of the Lord was with them. When Israel was in its right mind and its prayers went forth, the Lord fought for them, which is part of why the heathen nations, and Moab in particular, have hated Israel to this day.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: When they come to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rise up and smite the Moabites so that they flee, and Israel goes forward smiting them even into their own country, beating down cities, casting stones on every good piece of land, stopping the wells, and felling the good trees, leaving only the stones of Kir-haraseth, which the slingers went about and smote.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: When the king of Moab sees the battle is too sore for him, he takes seven hundred men with drawn swords to break through to the king of Edom, but they cannot. Then he takes his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead and offers him for a burnt offering upon the wall.

note.label: 2 Kings 3: Three Kings and the Water in the Ditches

points: There is great indignation against Israel, and they depart from him and return to their own land.
